paper_metadata.title: Quantum Attacks on Bitcoin, and How to Protect Against Them

summary: The paper analyzes quantum attacks on Bitcoin using Grover’s algorithm for proof‑of‑work and Shor’s algorithm for ECDSA signatures. They estimate that a Grover-based miner with ~2402 logical qubits and ~4.4×10^6 physical qubits would achieve only ~13.8 GH/s—about 1000× slower than modern ASIC miners (~14 TH/s). In contrast, Shor’s algorithm could break Bitcoin’s 256‑bit ECDSA with ~2334 logical qubits and ~1.7×10^6 physical qubits, taking ~6.5 days at 66 MHz or ~30 minutes at 10 GHz under optimistic assumptions.

experiments.description: Theoretical Grover-search attack on Bitcoin proof-of-work (Hashcash/SHA256^2) using a universal gate-based quantum computer, with resource estimates under surface-code error correction and superconducting-circuit assumptions.

algorithm.variant: Grover search for Bitcoin proof-of-work preimage search

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Search over well-formed block headers by varying nonce, transactions, and timestamp bits; Grover oracle marks headers whose double-SHA256 hash is below target t.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Find block header h such that SHA256(SHA256(header)) <= t
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Oracle predicate on valid headers; no penalty formulation

problem_instance.description: Bitcoin proof-of-work mining on current/near-term network difficulty; analysis includes D = 10^12 and D = 10^13 examples and extrapolated future difficulty.

dataset_specification.description: Difficulty and hash-rate extrapolated from blockchain.info data; current difficulty and future projections used for resource estimates

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Model assumes random oracle behavior for SHA256 and uses extrapolated Bitcoin network hash-rate/difficulty curves from historical blockchain.info data
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Analytical resource estimation; no empirical runs

noise_model.noise_type: surface-code fault-tolerant model with physical gate errors

implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Construct deterministic mapping g from bitstrings to well-formed block headers; use random-oracle model for SHA256
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Measure candidate header and verify hash condition classically
implementation_details.total_execution_time: Analytical estimates only; example runtime 13.8 GH/s effective hash rate at D=10^12, pg=5e-4, s=66.7MHz

results.unit: T gates logical depth factor per oracle call

speedup_claims.conditions: Grover search in the random oracle model
speedup_claims.caveats: Quantum advantage is reduced or negated by slow gate speeds and error-correction overhead; at current difficulty and near-term hardware, the paper argues no practical advantage.

speedup_claims.conditions: if quantum gate speeds reach 100 GHz
speedup_claims.caveats: Described as unlikely in the next decade.
Parallelization changes the constant factor but not the asymptotic quadratic nature.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(sqrt(N)) oracle queries for unstructured search; effective hash rate scales as O(s*sqrt(D)/c_tau)
complexity_analysis.total_operations_classical: Expected 2^256/t hashes (or D*2^32 in Bitcoin difficulty notation)
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_quantum: Example: 13.8 GH/s effective hash rate at D=10^12, pg=5e-4, s=66.7MHz; 2.0e3 TH/s under optimistic 50GHz/no-distillation assumptions
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_classical: Example ASIC hash rate 14 TH/s cited for comparison

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not reached in projections; classical ASIC miners remain faster than projected quantum hardware for the foreseeable decade.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: ≈4.4×10^6 physical qubits, surface-code error correction, ~66.7 MHz logical gate speed just to reach 13.8 GH/s effective hash rate (still ~1000× slower than ASIC miners at 14 TH/s).
limiting_factors: Slow logical gate speeds compared with ASIC hashing throughput

notes: This is a theoretical resource-estimation experiment, not an empirical hardware run.
Physical qubit count 4.4e6 is reported for D=10^12, pg=5e-4, s=66.7MHz; logical qubits are 2402.
The authors explicitly conclude that Bitcoin PoW is relatively resistant to quantum speedup in the next decade.
Even with optimistic assumptions the effective hash rate remains far below classical ASIC miners.

experiments.description: Theoretical Grover-search attack on Bitcoin proof-of-work using multiple quantum processors in parallel, with resource scaling for parallelization.

algorithm.variant: Grover search with parallel quantum processors

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Same Bitcoin block-header search space as the single-processor Grover attack
problem_formulation.objective_function: Find valid block header satisfying PoW target

problem_instance.description: Parallelized Bitcoin PoW attack analysis over the same SHA256^2 search problem

dataset_specification.description: Analytical scaling with d quantum processors

speedup_claims.conditions: d quantum processors acting in parallel
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a parallelization constant-factor improvement; the underlying search remains Grover-like.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(sqrt(N/d)) oracle scaling under parallel Grover search
complexity_analysis.constant_factor_quantum: Expected oracle calls reduced by factor 0.39/sqrt(d)

notes: Parallelization result is analytical; no separate hardware platform is specified.

experiments.description: Theoretical Shor-based attack on Bitcoin ECDSA signatures (secp256k1), estimating time and qubit resources to recover private keys from published public keys.

algorithm.variant: Shor algorithm for elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Quantum algorithm for ECDLP on 256-bit elliptic curve; no QUBO/Ising encoding
problem_formulation.objective_function: Find private key m from public key on elliptic curve

problem_instance.description: Bitcoin ECDSA signature scheme on secp256k1; attack scenarios include reused addresses, processed transactions, and unprocessed transactions
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Analytical resource estimation; example runtimes at 66.6 MHz and 10 GHz with different physical gate error rates

quantum_resources.error_correction.total_physical_qubits: ≈1.7×10^6 qubits (baseline) and ≈485,550 qubits in improved 10 GHz, pg=10^-5 scenario

noise_model.noise_type: surface-code fault-tolerant model with physical gate errors

implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Recover private key from public key; use it to forge a replacement transaction in the unprocessed-transaction attack scenario
implementation_details.total_execution_time: 6.49 days at 66.6 MHz clock speed with pg=5×10^-4; ~30 minutes with 10 GHz clock and pg=10^-5

speedup_claims.conditions: Shor algorithm on a sufficiently large universal quantum computer
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper emphasizes that the attack is practical only if large fault-tolerant quantum hardware exists; runtime depends strongly on clock speed and physical gate error rate.

speedup_claims.factor: breaks signature in less than 10 minutes as early as 2027
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a forecast, not an experimental demonstration.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Polynomial-time Shor attack on ECDLP; resource scaling dominated by O(n^3) Toffoli gates
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Believed hard classically; no efficient classical algorithm known
complexity_analysis.wall_clock_quantum: 6.49 days (66.6 MHz, pg=5e-4) or 30 minutes (10 GHz, pg=1e-5)

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: ECDLP instances on 256‑bit curves such as secp256k1 (Bitcoin).
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: ≈2334 logical qubits, ≈1.7×10^6 physical qubits with surface code, ~1.28×10^11 Toffoli gates; projected runtime 6.49 days at 66.6 MHz or ~30 minutes at 10 GHz with lower error rates.
limiting_factors: Dependence on extremely high clock speeds and low error rates

notes: The paper gives logical-qubit and physical-qubit estimates plus runtime examples; no specific QPU device is used.
The paper argues that Shor’s algorithm could break Bitcoin’s elliptic‑curve signatures within minutes once sufficiently large fault‑tolerant quantum computers exist.
They estimate attacks possibly feasible around 2027 under optimistic scaling.

experiments.description: Theoretical quantum attack on Momentum proof-of-work, showing that a gate-based quantum computer gains less than quadratic advantage because collision finding is required.

algorithm.variant: Grover search over Momentum-style proof-of-work with collision subroutine

hyperparameters.quantum_lower_bound: collision testing requires at least |S|^(2/3) time

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Search for H,a,b such that h1(H||a||b) <= t and h2(H||a)=h2(H||b)
problem_formulation.objective_function: Find a valid Momentum proof-of-work witness (H,a,b)
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Collision condition plus hash threshold condition

problem_instance.description: Momentum memory-hard proof-of-work proposal analyzed as a quantum-resistant alternative to Bitcoin PoW

dataset_specification.description: Abstract hash-function model with parameters n, ell, t, and subset S

results.unit: T = sqrt(2^(n+ell)/t) at optimal memory setting

speedup_claims.factor: no quadratic quantum advantage; fastest quantum algorithm is at least T^(2/3)
speedup_claims.conditions: for subset size S larger than constant size
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a lower-bound analysis, not a concrete implementation or hardware run.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: At least T^(2/3) for the fastest quantum algorithm under the paper's analysis
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: T or T*|S| depending on memory regime; optimal classical runtime T = sqrt(2^(n+ell)/t)

notes: This section is a theoretical lower-bound analysis; no explicit qubit count or circuit resource estimate is provided.

experiments.description: Theoretical analysis of a quantum attack on the Momentum proof-of-work scheme showing reduced quantum speedup relative to Bitcoin’s hash-based PoW.

algorithm.variant: Quantum collision/element-distinctness based search using Ambainis algorithm and Grover search bounds

key_results: Classical optimal runtime T = sqrt(2^(n+ℓ)/t) with memory size sqrt(2^(n+ℓ)/t).
Quantum lower bound for testing candidate H requires |S|^(2/3) queries (Aaronson–Shi collision lower bound).
Overall quantum runtime lower bound ≥ T^(2/3), meaning quantum advantage is significantly less than quadratic.
